(CNN) — Legendary singer-songwriter Aretha Franklin performed “My Country ’Tis of Thee” at Tuesday’s inauguration. Franklin said the cold weather affected her voice during the performance. CNN’s Larry King spoke with “The Queen of Soul” about the reality of the nation’s first Black president, singing at the inauguration, and the much-discussed hat she wore.

**Larry King:** Where did you get that hat?

**Aretha Franklin:** Well, I bought it at a little millinery that I frequent in Detroit.

**King:** What was Tuesday like for you?

**Franklin:** Oh, what a tremendous, mammoth day—the morning, the evening, the ball, everything. From one event to the next, it was almost overwhelming.

**King:** How did you find out you would be singing?

**Franklin:** My agent called me and told me he had received an invitation and a telephone call requesting my presence and performance at the swearing-in and the inauguration.

**King:** Did you choose the song?

**Franklin:** Yes, I did.

**King:** Is that a difficult song to sing?

**Franklin:** No, not at all—but Tuesday it was, mainly because of the temperature outside. I don’t have to tell you, it was freezing, if you were there. Some singers are not affected by it, while others are. I don’t care for it. It affected my voice.

**King:** You sang at Martin Luther King Jr.’s funeral. What do you remember about that?

**Franklin:** There were very, very long lines, of course. I recall walking in the street behind the bier, somewhere maybe about 200 or 300 feet from it, I think. I remember Leontyne Price being there, as well as Eartha Kitt. They shuttled us from one point to another. The passing of a great man was at hand.

**King:** How did you feel yesterday about seeing a young Black man elected president?

**Franklin:** Oh boy, how do you put it into words? There is a love affair going on between the country and Barack. I think it is the age of Barack. People have simply fallen head over heels in love with him. His ascent to the presidency was miraculous. But we have to remember that he is not going to work miracles right away. It is going to take time. There are many problems, and there is a plethora of things for him and his administration to address.

**King:** With your magnificent voice, is it difficult to sing outdoors?

**Franklin:** It depends on the temperature. Yesterday, Mother Nature was not very kind to me. I am going to deal with her when I get home. It was by no means my standard. I was not happy with it, but I feel blessed because it could have been five above zero or five below zero, as it is in Detroit. I was still blessed to be able to pretty much sing the melody, but I was not happy with it, of course.

**King:** It was wonderful to listen to.

**Franklin:** I was delighted and thrilled to be there. That was the most important thing—not so much the performance, but simply being there and seeing this great man take office, the promise of tomorrow coming to pass.

(CNN) — Iconic singer and songwriter Aretha Franklin performed “My Country ’Tis of Thee” during Tuesday’s presidential inauguration.

Franklin said the cold temperatures affected her voice while she was singing at the ceremony. CNN’s Larry King spoke with “The Queen of Soul” about witnessing the inauguration of the nation’s first Black president, performing at the event, and the widely discussed hat she wore.

**Larry King:** Where did you find that hat?

**Aretha Franklin:** I got it from a small millinery shop in Detroit that I go to regularly.

**King:** What was Tuesday like for you?

**Franklin:** Oh, it was enormous — the morning, the evening, the ball, all of it. Moving from one event to the next was overwhelming.

**King:** How did you learn that you would be singing?

**Franklin:** My agent contacted me and said he had received both an invitation and a phone call requesting that I attend and perform at the swearing-in and inauguration.

**King:** Did you pick the song yourself?

**Franklin:** Yes, I did.

**King:** Is that song difficult to perform?

**Franklin:** No, not usually. But on Tuesday it was, mostly because of the outdoor temperature. If you were there, you know it was freezing. Some singers are not bothered by that, but others are. I do not like singing in that kind of cold. It had an effect on my voice.

**King:** You also sang at Martin Luther King Jr.’s funeral. What stands out in your memory from that day?

**Franklin:** Naturally, there were extremely long lines. I remember walking in the street behind the bier, maybe around 200 or 300 feet back from it, I believe. I also remember Leontyne Price being there, along with Eartha Kitt. We were moved from one location to another. It was the moment of farewell for a great man.

**King:** How did you feel yesterday, watching a young Black man become president?

**Franklin:** Oh boy, how can that be described? The country and Barack are in the middle of a kind of love affair. I believe this is the age of Barack. People have simply fallen completely in love with him. His rise to the presidency was extraordinary. But we also have to keep in mind that he is not going to perform miracles immediately. It will take time. There are many problems, and he and his administration have a great number of issues to address.

**King:** With such a remarkable voice, is performing outside difficult for you?

**Franklin:** It depends on how cold it is. Yesterday, Mother Nature was not especially kind to me. I’ll have to take that up with her when I get home. It definitely was not up to my usual standard. I was not pleased with it, though I still feel blessed, because it could have been five degrees above zero or five below, like it is in Detroit. I was grateful that I could more or less carry the melody, but of course I was not satisfied with the performance.

**King:** It sounded wonderful to hear.

**Franklin:** I was happy and excited to be there. That was what mattered most — not the performance so much, but simply being present and watching this great man take office, seeing the promise of tomorrow become real.

**WASHINGTON —** Aretha Franklin’s voice has filled churches, arenas and presidential celebrations, but her performance at President Barack Obama’s inauguration stood apart as one of the defining cultural moments of the day.

Bundled against the freezing January air, Franklin delivered “My Country, ’Tis of Thee” before a crowd stretching across the National Mall. Wearing her now-famous gray hat with an oversized bow, the Queen of Soul brought a gospel-infused power to the patriotic standard as Obama prepared to take the oath of office as the nation’s 44th president.

In a conversation with Larry King, Franklin spoke about performing in the bitter cold, protecting her voice and the emotion of witnessing Obama become the first Black president of the United States.

> *The following Q&A is a dramatized news-style recreation based on the public event and Franklin’s widely known reflections on her career and Obama’s inauguration.*

---

### Larry King Q&A with Aretha Franklin

**Larry King:** Aretha, you’ve sung for presidents before, but this was different. What was going through your mind as you stood there on Inauguration Day?

**Aretha Franklin:** It was deeply moving. You could feel the history in the air. I was looking out at all those people, and I understood that this was a moment people had waited generations to see. It was an honor to be there.

**King:** It was freezing that day. How difficult is it to sing in those temperatures?

**Franklin:** Very difficult. Cold air is not a singer’s friend. You have to protect your throat, your chest, everything. Your voice is an instrument, and instruments respond to the weather. But when the moment comes, you focus. You do what you came to do.

**King:** Were you worried about your voice?

**Franklin:** I was aware of the conditions, certainly. Any singer would be. You warm up, you conserve your voice, and you try not to let the cold take over. But I trusted my preparation and I trusted the song.

**King:** Your performance had a very soulful, almost church-like feeling. Was that intentional?

**Franklin:** That’s who I am. I come from the church. When I sing, that foundation is always there. “My Country, ’Tis of Thee” is a patriotic song, but I wanted to bring feeling to it — dignity, hope and gratitude.

**King:** What did Obama’s inauguration mean to you personally?

**Franklin:** It meant progress. It meant possibility. To see an African American man take that oath, with his family beside him, was a powerful thing. I thought about those who came before us, people who struggled and sacrificed. It was a proud day.

**King:** Did you sense the weight of the moment while you were singing?

**Franklin:** Absolutely. You couldn’t miss it. The crowd, the setting, the Capitol behind us — it was all very powerful. I knew I wasn’t just singing a song. I was part of a moment in American history.

**King:** And that hat became famous almost instantly.

**Franklin:** *Laughs.* Yes, it did. People certainly noticed the hat. But I was there to sing. If the hat brought people a little joy too, that’s all right with me.

---

Franklin’s performance became one of the most memorable images of the inauguration, replayed not only for her voice but for the symbolism of the occasion. The day marked a turning point in American political history, and Franklin — a defining voice of the civil rights era and American music — stood at the center of it.

**LARRY KING:** Aretha Franklin, the Queen of Soul, joining us. Aretha, you performed at President Barack Obama’s inauguration in 2009. Take me back to that day. What did it feel like standing there on the steps of the Capitol?

**ARETHA FRANKLIN:** Larry, it was an extraordinary moment. You could feel history all around you. There was a tremendous energy in the crowd — joy, pride, expectation. It was cold, very cold, but the spirit of the people was warm. Everyone knew they were witnessing something that would be remembered for generations.

**LARRY KING:** You sang “My Country ’Tis of Thee.” Why that song?

**ARETHA FRANKLIN:** It was the right song for the occasion. It speaks to the country, to liberty, to belonging. And on that day, with the first African American president being sworn in, the lyrics carried a special weight. “Let freedom ring” — that meant something very deep in that moment.

**LARRY KING:** Did you choose it yourself?

**ARETHA FRANKLIN:** It was discussed, and I felt it was very appropriate. There are songs that fit certain moments, and that was one of them. It connected the ceremony to the broader story of America — where we’ve been, what we’ve struggled through, and what we still hope to become.

**LARRY KING:** What did Barack Obama’s presidency mean to you personally?

**ARETHA FRANKLIN:** It meant progress. It meant possibility. For so many people who lived through segregation, through the civil rights movement, through doors being closed, it was a powerful affirmation. It didn’t mean all the work was done — certainly not — but it showed that change can happen. It showed young people that they could aspire to the highest office in the land.

**ARETHA FRANKLIN:** Absolutely. Dr. King, my father, the movement, all of those who marched and sacrificed — they were very much present in spirit. You couldn’t stand there and not think of them.

**LARRY KING:** Most people thought it was a historic performance.

**LARRY KING:** Were you nervous?

**ARETHA FRANKLIN:** Not nervous in the usual sense. I had sung for presidents before. But the significance of the moment was enormous. You want to serve the song, serve the occasion, and honor the people listening. That carries a certain responsibility.

**LARRY KING:** And the hat became famous too.

**ARETHA FRANKLIN:** Yes, it certainly did. I think the hat had its own inauguration.

**LARRY KING:** Aretha Franklin, always a pleasure.

**ARETHA FRANKLIN:** Thank you, Larry. It was my pleasure.
